As we have already mentioned throughout the module, using GenAI in academic work does not change who is responsible for the work produced. You are responsible for the whole process: from how you decide to use GenAI for, to what you submit. 

Always keep in mind these five principles of academic integrity:
Be honest about how you use GenAI. Which platforms did you use? For what specific exercises? How did you evaluate the output? What, if anything, did you incorporate into your own work?
Check AI-generated information, conclusions, reasoning, and references. Do not accept it just because it sounds plausible or because it confirms what you expected.
Keep track of how you use AI for your academic work, even if it’s not explicitly required in a course.

Tasks and assignments are designed to make you think and develop your own learning. Do not delegate that to AI. Remember: the beginning is always yours, and the ending is always yours. Start with your own thinking and critically evaluate what GenAI contributes before deciding what to incorporate into your work. Ask yourself: 1) Are the core ideas and judgments in this assignment mine? and 2) Would I be able to do this without the help of GenAI?

You remain fully responsible for the work you submit. You must ensure that your work is your own, verify the accuracy of information and references, and be able to explain and defend your arguments and conclusions.

c3.block-1.Text 1: C1 covered what GenAI is. C2 covered what it is to us. C3 covers the operational layer: how we actually interact with it. This is not a collection of prompt tips — it is a framework built around one cycle.

c3.block-4.Text 1: A prompt is a text input given to AI to instruct a task. Research defines prompt engineering as "the skill of articulating a problem, its context, and the constraints of the desired solution to an AI assistant" (Federiakin et al., 2024).
c3.block-4.Text 3: . It is the act of defining what you want to do, what you expect, what process to follow, and under what conditions. Think of it as designing a virtual workspace where AI operates on your terms. To write a good prompt, you need to understand GenAI, but you also need to understand yourself: your task, your intention, your current stage, and your boundaries.

c3.block-5.Text 1: "Learning how to interact with AI is not unlike being someone who's really good at asking questions. Prompting AI is very similar. You can't just randomly ask a bunch of questions. Asking AI to be an assistant to you requires some expertise and artistry of how to prompt it."
c3.block-5.Text 2: — Jensen Huang, CEO of NVIDIA (Cleo Abram, "Huge Conversations", January 2025)

c3.block-6.Text 1: Six types of information AI uses to process a task

c3.block-7.Text 1: Research consistently shows that AI performs significantly better when certain types of information are clearly provided. The following six are the key components that support how AI processes and responds to your request.

c3.block-9.Text 4: . The more you specify the purpose, scope, context, and conditions of a task, the narrower AI's working space becomes.
c3.block-9.Text 5: AI interprets the task in the most generic way possible. Whether it matches your intent is left to chance.
c3.block-9.Text 6: Consensus: treated as baseline across all major prompt engineering surveys

c3.extra-0.Text 3: › C3 · How Do We Use AI?

c3.block-10.Text 4: . Setting a role is not a technique to boost AI accuracy — it is the act of deciding what position you want AI to occupy for this task.
c3.block-10.Text 5: AI operates as a generic "helpful assistant."
c3.block-10.Text 6: Evidence: no measurable accuracy improvement on benchmarks (Zheng et al., 2024 EMNLP; 162 personas, 4 LLM families). Effective as a tone and framing tool.
c3.block-10.Emphasis 1: what perspective AI should operate from

c3.block-11.Text 4: . When you throw a complex task at AI in one piece, you cannot tell which part of the output went wrong.
c3.block-11.Text 5: AI decomposes the task on its own, but you cannot know if its decomposition matches your intent.
c3.block-11.Text 6: Evidence: Least-to-Most prompting showed 83.5pp gain on compositional benchmarks (Zhou et al., 2022 ICLR)

c3.block-12.Text 4: . The act of creating an example forces you to check: do I actually know what I want? Modern models can infer intent without examples, but that means the model interprets on its own.
c3.block-12.Text 5: AI responds in its most generic form. Without a standard, you cannot judge if it is right.
c3.block-12.Text 6: Evidence: established in Brown et al. (2020, NeurIPS) GPT-3 paper. Few-shot CoT scored highest in Schulhoff et al. benchmarks.
c3.block-12.Emphasis 1: what the desired output looks like

c3.block-13.Text 4: . Asking AI to show its intermediate steps opens a window for you to check its logic.
c3.block-13.Text 5: You get only the conclusion, with no visibility into how it got there. If it sounds plausible, you just accept it.
c3.block-13.Text 6: Evidence: Wei et al. (2022, NeurIPS) GSM8K 18% → 58%. However, effects are limited outside math/symbolic reasoning (Sprague et al., 2024).

c3.block-14.Text 4: . The same content delivered as a table, a list, a single sentence, or a set of questions changes how you can use it afterward. Specifying the format is not a convenience — it is designing how the output will integrate into your workflow.
c3.block-14.Text 5: AI defaults to its standard form (usually long paragraphs).
c3.block-14.Text 6: Revisited in Section 3 (Integrate) from the integration strategy perspective.

c3.block-16.Text 1: If you think through these components before prompting, you stay in control of the task. If you skip them, AI fills them in for you, and because its output looks plausible, you may not realize decisions were made without you. Having your own ideas about these components before you let AI work is what we call proactive GenAI usage.

c3.block-26.Heading 1: Output is not an answer — it is a candidate

c3.block-27.Text 1: What AI gives you is not a final answer but a
c3.block-27.Text 2: : candidate structure, candidate wording, candidate comparison, candidate interpretation. Output is material to review, not material to adopt.
c3.block-27.Text 3: This connects directly to what you learned in C1. GenAI output is statistically likely, not factually verified. It is conditioned on prior tokens, not on reasoning. It is bounded by training data. It reflects a distribution, not authorship. Without your domain knowledge, critique is impossible.

c3.block-34.Heading 1: How AI output enters your work

c3.block-35.Text 1: Integration does not start after you receive the output — it starts at the prompting stage. The moment you decide what format to receive the output in, you have already determined how safe and controllable the integration will be.
c3.block-35.Text 2: "Compare these papers" produces paragraphs that easily bleed into your writing. "Make a comparison table" keeps the output separate from your text, verifiable cell by cell. Choosing the output format is not a convenience — it is a

c3.block-36.Text 1: Highest risk of blending into your writing. Use with caution.
c3.block-36.Table text 4: Verifiable and extractable cell by cell. Does not blend into your prose.
c3.block-36.Table text 6: Serves as a thinking prompt. No copy-paste risk. You have to write the answers.
c3.block-36.Table text 8: A single claim — easy to accept or reject clearly.
c3.block-36.Table text 10: Easy to selectively adopt. You write the sentences.
c3.block-36.Table text 12: Use the structure as reference; fill in the content yourself.

c3.block-39.Text 2: Break the output into units that can be judged independently. Rows for tables, items for lists, claims for paragraphs.

c3.block-44.Text 1: Use GenAI responsibly during your study work, make sure you adhere to the ESSB principles and Guidelines.

c3.block-46.Text 1: AI processes structured input more accurately than prose paragraphs. Formatting changes alone can shift accuracy by up to 76 percentage points (Sclar et al., ICLR 2024). Two common structuring formats are Markdown and XML.

c3.block-48.Text 5: for lists — intuitive and easy for humans to read. XML uses explicit opening and closing tags, which models parse more precisely. XML is the only delimiter format recommended by all three major providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google), making it advantageous for complex prompts.

c3.block-54.Text 9: Place key instructions at the edges
c3.block-54.Text 10: Put the most important instructions at the very beginning or very end of your prompt, countering the "Lost in the Middle" effect (Liu et al., 2024).
